title.text: Giving a model your knowledge: retrieval-augmented generation, long context and fine-tuning

objects.text: How do I give an AI model my company’s knowledge, and when is each way worth it?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 9 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 9. Last time you learned to write a strong prompt and to test it. But a prompt can only work with what the model already holds, and the model has not read your handbook, your contracts or your price lists. So our question today is this: how do I give an AI model my company’s knowledge, and when is each way worth it?

You see three ways, in the order a sensible company tries them: prompting, retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning, with real numbers from real runs on a handbook.

slides.notes:
To answer that question, here is what you leave with today. You can describe three ways to give a model your knowledge (prompting, retrieval-augmented generation and fine-tuning) and the order to try them. You can read the real scores of a retrieval step and say where it can miss.

And you can use a decision tree to choose between prompting, RAG and fine-tuning for a request from your own job. Nothing to hand in and nothing to be tested on.

title.text: Your two hours: prompting, RAG and fine-tuning

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_9f226eb2.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Thirty-five minutes of ideas, twenty-five of demonstrations, and a paper exercise.

slides.notes:
Here is how the two hours get you there. We start with a short recall of Session 8. Then comes the main part: three ways, prompting first, then retrieval-augmented generation, then fine-tuning, each with an everyday example and a real number. After that I run three demonstrations on the handbook of Nile Valley Foods.

You then work through a paper exercise without a computer, and we finish with what this means for your own job.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Name three parts of a strong prompt.
2.  Why ask a model for structured output?
3.  How does a reasoning model differ from a standard model?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png
objects.alt: Three questions

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 8. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Name three parts of a strong prompt. Take a moment.

A good answer is this. A role, the context, examples, the output format and the constraints; and you test the prompt on a checked set.

Question two. Why ask a model for structured output? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. The answer can then be checked and used by the next step without retyping.

Question three. How does a reasoning model differ from a standard model? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. It spends extra effort working through the problem before it answers. You frame the problem clearly rather than dictate every step.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_chain_11.90x4.45_60512c46.png

So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold embeddings and cosine similarity from Session 4 and a prompt with pasted text from Session 8. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: prompting, RAG or fine-tuning on your data.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 10: what still goes wrong, and how to check. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A retriever fetches relevant text from your documents, and the model answers from it.

Chunking, embedding, vector database. Cut documents into chunks. An embedding is numbers for meaning. A vector database stores them.

Retriever, top-k retrieval. The retriever scores every chunk against the question. Top-k keeps the k best.

Context window. The number of tokens a model can read at one time. Long context means a large window.

Fine-tuning, LoRA, adapter, rank. More training on your examples. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) trains a small adapter; rank sets its size.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
A model knows only what it learned in
training and what is in its context window

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_knowledge_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A model knows only what it learned in training and what is in its context window

objects.text: Your handbook was never in its training.

runs.text: Training stops at a cut-off date.
The context window holds your prompt and pasted text.
Your files stay unseen unless you supply them.

slides.notes:
You now have the five words, so let me show you the problem they solve. Think of a new accountant who has just left university. Clever, well read, and with no idea what your company decided last March. A model is in the same position. It learned from a huge amount of text up to a cut-off date, and it reads only what fits in its context window, the number of tokens it takes in at one time. Your handbook, price lists and contracts were never part of its training.

So today is about a single question: how does the model get to see your knowledge? There are three ways, and they differ in cost and in what they can do. Here they are on one page.

title.text:
Three ways to give a model your
knowledge: prompting, RAG and fine-tuning

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_ladder_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Three ways to give a model your knowledge: prompting, RAG and fine-tuning

objects.text: Source for the order: one vendor guide, checked 6 November 2026. See the notes.

slides.notes:
This is the plan for the whole session, and each way gets the same treatment: an everyday example, the proper term, a real number and, for most, a demonstration. First is prompting: you paste what the model needs into the prompt. Second is retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG: a retriever, which is a search step, fetches the right text from your documents before the model answers. Third is fine-tuning: more training that changes the model itself. Each costs more effort than the one before.

One vendor guide, from OpenAI, also says to start with prompting and a set of at least twenty checked questions, and to move on when the cheaper step falls short. That is advice from one vendor, and the logic is general: measure first.

title.text:
Prompting first: paste the page.
The handbook is only 1,074 tokens

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_tokens_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Prompting first: paste the page. The handbook is only 1,074 tokens

objects.text: A short document fits in a prompt, and no extra tooling is needed.

runs.text: A token is a word or part of a word, the unit a model reads.
829 words came to 1,074 tokens, about 1.3 a word.
That fits easily in a context window.

slides.notes:
Let us start with prompting, because the first question is whether you need to build anything at all. It costs nothing but care. If the answer lives in one short document, paste it into the prompt and ask. I counted the real tokens of four NVF documents with a standard counting tool. The staff handbook excerpt is eight hundred and twenty-nine words and ten hundred and seventy-four tokens.

That is about one and a third tokens a word. Models differ in how they count, so treat the figures as an order of size. Before you build anything, ask whether pasting would do. When it would not, you need a way to pick out the right pages.

title.text:
An open-book test shows the idea:
look in the index, then answer

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_openbook_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: An open-book test shows the idea: look in the index, then answer

objects.text: Think of it like a 300-page textbook you may use in a test.

runs.text: The whole book will not fit on your desk.
The index points to 3 pages.
You write the answer from those 3 pages.

slides.notes:
Before the technical version, an everyday one. Imagine an open-book test with a 300 page textbook. The question is why water boils at a lower temperature on a mountain. You cannot read the whole book in the time you have, and it will not fit on your desk. So you look in the index, which points to three pages: 112, 113 and 87. You read those three pages and write the answer from them.

The lower row names each step with its industry term. They are the same steps a computer follows, and the following slide shows them with real numbers. The comparison has one limit: you understand the pages, while a computer only matches them by similarity of meaning.

title.text:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): a retriever
fetches the top 3 chunks, then the model answers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_librarian_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): a retriever fetches the top 3 chunks, then the model answers

objects.text: Real run on the NVF staff handbook: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, 6 November 2026.

slides.notes:
That brings us to the technical version, retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. A chunk is one piece of the handbook, here one clause. As in Session 4, the question becomes an embedding, a list of numbers, and so does every chunk. The embeddings of the chunks are stored ahead of time in a vector database, which can find the nearest ones quickly. The retriever scores each chunk against the question and keeps the top three, which is top-k retrieval with k equal to three. The model then writes the answer from those chunks.

In this real run, clause 3.2 scores 0.73 and the answer is the Finance Manager. The open-book analogy breaks in one place: the retriever matches similarity and does not understand. So how do we cut the handbook?

title.text:
Chunking: where you cut the document
decides what the retriever can find

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_chunks_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Chunking: where you cut the document decides what the retriever can find

objects.text: Chunking is cutting a document into chunks. Cut badly and a rule is split in two.

runs.text: By clause: 30 chunks, 8 of 8 right.
Every 150 characters: 5 of 8 right.

slides.notes:
The retriever can only fetch the chunks we made, so chunking is a quiet step that decides a lot. Cut a recipe through the middle of its ingredients and the index points to half a recipe. I ran the same eight questions three ways. Cutting by clause kept every rule whole, and the top hit held the whole answer in eight of eight questions. Cutting every one hundred and fifty characters split clause three point two in half, the answer sat in the second chunk, and the top hit was the first.

That gave five of eight. Cutting every three hundred characters also gave eight of eight on this small file. So the lesson is to look at your chunks, and test. Once the chunks exist, the system has to rank them.

title.text:
Peek inside the score: the dot
product of two embeddings

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_peek_score_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Peek inside the score: the dot product of two embeddings

objects.text: Recorded run, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, 6 Nov 2026. Script: peek_scoring.py.

slides.notes:
Here is what the score really is: the dot product from Session 4. With three numbers, (1, 2, 3) and (2, 0, 1) give 1 times 2, plus 2 times 0, plus 3 times 1, which is 5. The formula is score equals q1 c1 plus q2 c2 and so on, where q is a number of the question embedding and c is the matching number of the chunk.

Here each list has 384 numbers; I show the first six. Minus 0.059 times minus 0.045 gives 0.0027. Adding all 384 products gives 0.73 for clause 3.2 and 0.47 for clause 3.1. The lists are scaled to length one, so the sum is the cosine similarity: cosine theta equals q dot c, divided by the length of q times the length of c. Only the final sums, compared, mean anything.

title.text: Top-k retrieval ranks the chunks: 0.73 beats 0.47

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_scores_q03_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Top-k retrieval ranks the chunks: 0.73 beats 0.47

objects.text: The cosine scores from the peek, now used to rank the clauses.

runs.text: Cosine similarity: 1.00 means identical meaning.
Gap for Q03: 0.73 minus 0.47 is 0.26.
Top-k keeps the k best; here k is 3.

slides.notes:
You have just seen how one score is made, so now we use it to rank. As in Session 4, a score of one means identical meaning. For the question about who approves a claim of UGX 1,500,000, clause three point two scores zero point seven three. The next clause, about receipts, scores zero point four seven.

The gap is zero point two six. Top-k retrieval keeps the k chunks with the largest cosine, here k equal to three, and hands them to the model. These are the real numbers from the run. Now let me show you the whole ranking, for all ten questions.

title.text:
Demonstration: the retriever
on all ten handbook questions

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_retrieval_table_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: the retriever on all ten handbook questions

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: 8 of 8 answerable questions: the right clause comes first
Q08 scores only 0.40 and is still first
Q09 scores 0.70 and has no answer

slides.notes:
One question is a good start, so I run the retriever on all ten. The thirty chunk embeddings sit in a plain in-memory array here; a vector database does the same job for millions. This is a real run you can repeat. I cut the handbook into thirty clauses, embedded them and the ten questions, and listed the closest clause for each. For the eight questions that the handbook answers, the right clause came first every time. Question eight, about accommodation, scored only zero point four zero, and it was still first.

Watch the last two rows. Those questions have no answer in the handbook, yet question nine still scores zero point seven zero. Keep that in mind for what follows.

title.text:
The closest page is not always an
answer, so let the model say so

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_miss_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The closest page is not always an answer, so let the model say so

objects.text: A high score means the topics are close. It does not mean the answer is there.

runs.text: Q09 asks for paid sick days. The handbook does not say.
0.70 for leave clause 2.1, against 0.73 for the real answer to Q03.

slides.notes:
What did you notice in those last two rows? A clause came back even where the handbook has no answer. That is a retrieval limit you must know.

Question nine asks how many days of paid sick leave staff get. The handbook gives no number. Yet the closest clause, annual leave, scores zero point seven zero, almost the same as the zero point seven three for a question that does have an answer. So a score alone cannot tell you whether the answer is present. In the recorded runs the assistant read the pages and wrote not stated. That is why your instructions must allow that answer, and why you test it.

title.text:
The same questions with no handbook,
three retrieved chunks, and the whole text

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_with_without_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The same questions with no handbook, three retrieved chunks, and the whole text

objects.text: Scored on the answer key. Recorded runs: Claude, fresh sessions, 4 and 6 November 2026.

slides.notes:
Let me show you what the recorded runs did with those pages. This is the same question with and without the document, as recorded runs. With no handbook text, the assistant said not stated for all ten questions, in two runs, and it invented nothing. That earns two right answers, only because questions nine and ten are really not stated.

With three retrieved clauses it scored ten of ten in two runs. With the whole handbook pasted in, ten of ten in two runs. These are fresh Claude sessions, not ChatGPT or Gemini, and another product may behave differently.

title.text:
Long context lets you paste a lot,
but the context window has limits

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_context_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Long context lets you paste a lot, but the context window has limits

objects.text: The context window is the number of tokens a model can read and write at once.

runs.text: Researchers report that facts in the middle of a long input can be missed.
Longer input costs more and takes longer.

slides.notes:
Those runs pasted a short file, so what if the file is very long? That is the question long context answers. Many models now accept long inputs, so you can paste a whole contract. That is prompting stretched, with limits. A published study by Liu and colleagues found that models often used the start and the end of a long input better than the middle. That was in their tests, so I draw the shape and give no numbers.

Longer inputs cost more and take longer, and everything you paste is sent to the model, so check Session 13 first. One rule sets the limit: prompt plus retrieved text plus answer must be no more than the context window. For Q03, 94 plus 104 plus 300 is 498 tokens by retrieval, against 1,468 with the whole handbook pasted. So when do you paste, and when do you retrieve?

title.text:
Long context (paste everything)
or RAG (retrieve the chunks)?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.75.png
objects.alt: doc

objects.text: Long context

runs.text: One short file, like a 1,074 token handbook
Easy to set up
Answers use the whole text

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.75.png
objects.alt: magnifier

objects.text: RAG

runs.text: Many files, or files that change
Only the top chunks are sent
Needs chunking and a test set

objects.text: Paste what fits and still answers well. Retrieve when it does not.

slides.notes:
So which one, paste the whole document or retrieve the chunks? If your knowledge is one short file, paste it. Anthropic makes the same point in its write-up on retrieval: for a small knowledge base you can simply put it all in the prompt. If you have hundreds of files, or files that change every week, RAG keeps the prompt small and the cost down, and it can point to the source clause.

It needs more care: chunking, scores and a test set. The decision is empirical. Try the simple way, measure, and climb if it falls short. Both of those bring documents to the model. The third way does something different.

title.text:
Fine-tuning continues training on your
examples to change the model’s habits

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_lora_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Fine-tuning continues training on your examples to change the model’s habits

objects.text: Think of it like a tailor altering a ready-made suit: the cloth stays and alterations are added.

runs.text: LoRA (low-rank adaptation) freezes the weights and trains a small adapter.
Here: 48 replies; 294,912 of 124,439,808 weights, or 0.24 percent.

slides.notes:
Prompting and RAG bring documents to the model. Fine-tuning changes the model itself: it continues training on your own examples, as in the post-training of Session 6. Think of a tailor with a ready-made suit. The cloth stays as it is and small alterations are added to make it fit. LoRA, low-rank adaptation, works like that. It comes from a 2021 paper by Hu and colleagues. It freezes the original weights and trains a small adapter added beside them.

In my run on a small open model, forty-eight example replies trained only 294,912 weights, which is 0.24 percent of the total. Let me open it up and show where that number comes from.

title.text:
Peek inside LoRA: an adapter of rank
8 adds 24,576 weights per block

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_lora_peek_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Peek inside LoRA: an adapter of rank 8 adds 24,576 weights per block

objects.text: GPT-2 small, LoRA rank 8. Recorded run: demo_runs/s09/lora_output.txt.

slides.notes:
Fine-tuning is the training loop of Session 0 on a model that already exists: predict, measure the loss, adjust the weights. Changing all 124 million weights would be slow, so LoRA freezes the original and adds two thin matrices, B and A, beside one weight matrix in each block.

The original has 768 by 2,304 weights, about 1.8 million. The adapter has a rank, here 8, the narrow width shared by B and A. B holds 768 by 8, A holds 8 by 2,304, together 24,576. In symbols, the new matrix W prime equals W plus B times A, and the trainable count is r times d plus k, here 8 times 3,072, against d times k.

Real LoRA also scales B A by a constant, left out here. Over twelve blocks that is 294,912, a quarter of one percent. Only those move.

title.text:
Demonstration: a tiny LoRA
learns a house sign-off

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_before_after_7.30x3.90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: a tiny LoRA learns a house sign-off

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Sign-off present: 0 of 6, then 6 of 6
Style is learned
Facts are invented: "Monday" and the name

slides.notes:
This is a real run of a tiny experiment on a small open model called GPT-2, with forty-eight invented replies in one house style. Watch two things: the sign-off, and the facts. Before training, none of six new messages got the house sign-off, and the text wandered. After training, all six ended with the sign-off. Now read the replies.

The model promised to arrive on Monday and greeted a Ms Nye, and nobody told it either. Other replies invented a cancellation on Wednesday. It learned the style. It did not learn facts. The model is tiny and the data is invented, so this shows the idea, not what a real product would do.

title.text: RAG supplies facts. Fine-tuning shapes habits.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.75.png
objects.alt: magnifier

objects.text: Use RAG for

runs.text: Facts that change
Answers that cite a clause
Private documents

runs.text: A steady format or tone at volume
A task the prompt cannot teach
Examples you own and may use

objects.text: Fine-tune only after prompting and RAG measurably fall short.

slides.notes:
What did you see in those six replies? The sign-off came back every time, and the facts did not. That gives us the rule. RAG supplies facts: the model reads the chunk and can cite the clause. Fine-tuning shapes habits: a tone, a format, a way of working. The same vendor guide I mentioned says use RAG when the model lacks knowledge, and fine-tuning when output is inconsistent or the format is wrong.

It also warns that the methods can be combined, but only if each earns its place. And the examples you train on must be yours to use, with personal data removed. One habit decides when to climb, and it comes next.

title.text:
Measure each method on ten checked
questions before you add the next

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t09_measure_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Measure each method on ten checked questions before you add the next

objects.text: Use the same ten questions and the same key every time.

runs.text: Two of ten here is two honest "not stated" answers.
A method earns its place only if it moves this score.

slides.notes:
Before you use that rule, one habit decides every step: measure each method. Remember the handbook runs. With no handbook the assistant scored two of ten, and those two are only the questions where not stated is the right answer. Pasting the text or retrieving three clauses scored ten of ten.

So on this set the cheapest method that works is pasting or retrieving, and fine-tuning would add nothing. Keep ten questions with known answers; the vendor guide suggests twenty or more for a serious test, and ten is a workable start. Run the cheap method, then the next, and compare.

Your own set may say something different. Session 10 turns this into a routine.

You have just made that choice for Nile Valley Foods; now make it for your own work. Take fifteen minutes. Pick one request where the model needs your knowledge: a policy question, a contract clause, a supplier price, a reply in your house style. Which method does it need?

Prompting only, if one short document will do. RAG, if the documents are many or change. Fine-tuning, if the style is the problem and you hold examples you may use. Or test first, if you cannot yet say how you would know the answer is right. Write the choice and the reason.

objects.text: Keep this page. Session 10 shows how to run the test set.

slides.notes:
You have now made the choice twice, so here is the page that puts it into three questions to keep. First, does a clearer prompt with the page pasted in give right answers on your ten questions?

If yes, stop. Second, are the facts too many, too long or changing?

Then use RAG, and look at your chunks. Third, is the style or format still wrong after the first two?

Then consider fine-tuning, with examples you own. At every step you measure on a checked set before you add the next method.
